content: To ensure proper citation in a word-processing program, it is recommended to place a unique character, such as an asterisk (), at the beginning of each citation. This character should not be used elsewhere in the text. If journal titles are abbreviated, they should conform to the abbreviations listed in the Index Medicus, which follows an international standard. The Index Medicus publishes its list of journals annually in the January issue. Unpublished observations should generally not be used as references. Papers that have been accepted for publication but are not yet published should be cited as in press or forthcoming. Research papers submitted to a journal but not yet accepted should be treated as unpublished observations. Authors should avoid citing personal communication unless it provides essential information unavailable from a public source. In such cases, the name of the individual and the date of communication should be cited in parentheses within the text. Authors must obtain permission and confirm the accuracy of the information from the source of the personal communication. Annex 4 provides examples of how to cite different types of references. The process of writing a scientific paper should begin before conducting the research, continue during the research, and conclude after the research results have been described, analyzed, and interpreted. After writing the paper, it should be carefully revised, first for content and then for style. Before starting the research, authors should search the literature and maintain a record of references, as well as prepare dummy tables for results. During the research, results should be recorded, and the literature should be updated. After completing the research, a systematic approach should be used to build the paper step by step, rather than attempting to write the entire paper at once. Authors should start with an outline to serve as a framework and begin with the easiest section, addressing individual sections one at a time. The discussion section requires the most careful thought and interpretation. Authors should decide on the journal to which the article will be submitted and study its format requirements. A rough draft should be written quickly without worrying about style, and the paper should then be set aside for several days or weeks before re-reading it. A version of the paper should be given to colleagues for review, and all drafts should be dated. When revising the manuscript for scientific content, authors should ensure the title is accurate, succinct, and effective. Keywords should be indexable, preferably using terms from the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) vocabulary of MEDLINE. The abstract should represent the content of all main sections of the paper within the journal's length requirements, and data in the abstract should agree with data in the paper. The introduction should adequately and concisely set the stage for the main question or hypothesis, which should be clear by the end of the introduction. Methods should be described in sufficient detail to allow replication of the research, including statistical methods. Results should be presented in a way that allows other investigators to verify and compare findings. Tables or illustrations should be omitted if unnecessary, and data in the text should agree with data in the tables. All tables and figures should be cited in the text and included, with correct legends. The discussion should properly interpret the significance of the data, reflect an up-to-date awareness of the literature, and justify conclusions based on the results. All references cited should be mentioned in the text, and all references mentioned in the text should be cited. The length of the paper should be appropriate, avoiding repetition of information and omitting unnecessary paragraphs or sentences. Concise papers are generally more effective, with an average manuscript being about 10 double-spaced pages or 3 published pages, including 25 references. The introduction and discussion sections are often too long, while the methods and results sections are often too short. A good rule is to shorten the introduction and discussion while expanding the methods and results sections. All pages should be numbered. When revising the manuscript for style, authors should follow the principle of KISS (Keep It Simple and Short). The simplest and shortest way of expressing an idea should be chosen. Writing a concise paper often takes more time than writing a lengthy one, but good planning can reduce the time spent writing. Self-editing should focus on paragraphs, sentences, and words. Well-structured paragraphs should include a topic sentence, body sentences that expand on the theme, and a transitional or concluding sentence. Paragraphs should not exceed 25 typed lines and should not be fewer than 5 or 6 lines. Sentences should avoid excessive length, ambiguity, verbosity, and unnecessary complexity. The active voice is generally clearer and easier to understand than the passive voice. Authors should avoid sexist language, slang, and jargon, and should follow the spelling style prescribed by the journal. Measurements should be reported in metric units, and hematological and clinical chemistry measurements should be reported in terms of the International System of Units (SI). Case reports are less commonly accepted for publication in major journals unless they provide unique or important new information. Examples of publishable case reports include those describing a previously undescribed syndrome or disease, an unexpected association of diseases, a significant variation from an expected pattern, or an unexpected therapeutic or adverse drug effect. A notable example is the 1981 report by Hymes et al. on eight cases of aggressive Kaposi’s sarcoma in young homosexual men, which first alerted the world to the AIDS epidemic. Secondary scientific papers, or review papers, summarize other studies and can be either narrative or systematic reviews. Narrative reviews are typically written by experts and provide updates on a subject without a systematic methodology. Systematic reviews, on the other hand, include explicit objectives, a defined research question, and a reproducible methodology for locating, selecting, and synthesizing data. Meta-analyses, a type of systematic review, statistically combine data from multiple studies to increase sample size and provide more precise estimates of effect. Results of meta-analyses are often presented in a standardized format, such as a forest plot, which visually represents the point estimates and confidence intervals of individual studies. A well-known example of the value of meta-analysis is the pooled analysis of seven trials on corticosteroid use in mothers at risk of preterm birth, which demonstrated a significant reduction in infant mortality.
